text.p: The following are the main stories from Friday morning's Austrian newspapers:
- New Interior Minister Karl Schloegl says he will continue the ideas of his predecessor Caspar Einem to integrate foreigners better. However, he will reduce the quota for new immigrants.
- The new owners of aluminium maker Amag want employees to work on Saturdays without higher pay.
- Telecommunications company tele.ring, jointly owned by federal railways OeBB and national grid Verbund, plans to begin operations by autumn 1997.
- Premiums for private insurance are to fall by five percent.

- Austrians welcome the change in the Social Democrat government team and see a coalition government including Joerg Haider's far-right Freedom Party as a possibility in the future, an opinion poll shows.
- Economics Minister Hannes Farnleitner has guaranteed electricity prices for households will not rise, as energy providers reduce the prices for industry.
- Creditanstalt says it does not envisage clients leaving the bank as a result of the bank's takeover by Bank Austria.
- Mineral water producer Roemerquelle's turnover fell 7.7 percent in 1996. Hopes are pinned on a new plastic bottle to be introduced this year.
- New Finance Minister Rudolf Edlinger hopes to convince all Austrians of his budget policies, rather than simply push his ideas through.
- As Austria's pensioners have a buying power of 250 billion schillings, pensions should be increased to raise demand in the country, social researcher Ernst Gehmacher says.
- Styria's Savings Bank plans a listing in 1998 by selling one billion schillings worth of shares.
- Austria's state-owned postal monopoly and the postal savings bank PSK have agreed that PSK can operate exclusively in Austria's 2,300 post offices over the next ten years.
